clinicalPearls: Descending pattern of weakness: facial muscles first (difficulty whistling, burying eyelashes on eye closure, drinking through a straw), then scapular fixators, then humeral muscles.
Striking left-right asymmetry of weakness is characteristic and helps distinguish it from most other dystrophies.
Scapular winging with a horizontal clavicle, upward-riding scapulae ('poly-hill' sign) and prominent axillary folds; biceps and triceps wasting with relative deltoid sparing gives a 'Popeye' arm.
Beevor's sign (upward movement of the umbilicus on neck flexion) reflects selective lower abdominal weakness and is a useful bedside clue.
Foot drop from early tibialis anterior involvement is common and a frequent cause of falls.
Extramuscular features include high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss and a retinal vasculopathy; severe infantile-onset disease may produce Coats disease.
Creatine kinase is usually normal or only mildly raised, and clinically significant cardiac involvement is uncommon compared with other muscular dystrophies.
Autosomal dominant inheritance, but de novo mutations and somatic mosaicism mean a negative family history does not exclude the diagnosis.
reference.pathophysiology: Facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy arises from aberrant, stable expression of the normally silenced DUX4 retrogene in skeletal muscle. In FSHD1 (the great majority of cases) a contraction of the D4Z4 macrosatellite repeat array on chromosome 4q35 reduces repeat number below a critical threshold, causing chromatin relaxation and hypomethylation that permit DUX4 transcription; disease only occurs when the contraction lies on a permissive 4qA haplotype that provides a polyadenylation signal stabilising the DUX4 transcript. In FSHD2 the array is of normal length but is hypomethylated because of loss-of-function variants in a chromatin modifier, most often SMCHD1 (occasionally DNMT3B), again on a permissive 4qA background, making it a digenic disorder. Misexpressed DUX4 is an early-embryonic transcription factor toxic to mature muscle, activating germline and apoptotic programmes and driving progressive, selective muscle degeneration.
additionalDifferentials: Scapuloperoneal syndromes and other scapuloperoneal myopathies
additionalInvestigations: Targeted molecular testing to size the D4Z4 repeat on 4q35 and determine the 4qA/4qB haplotype (molecular combing, optical genome mapping or Southern blot).
D4Z4 methylation analysis, particularly when FSHD2 is suspected.
SMCHD1 sequencing where FSHD2 or a hypomethylation pattern is identified.
Creatine kinase (typically normal or mildly elevated).
Muscle MRI demonstrating asymmetric, selective muscle involvement and guiding biopsy if needed.
Audiometry and dilated retinal examination, especially in early-onset or paediatric disease.
Electromyography to confirm a myopathic process and exclude neurogenic mimics.
redFlags: Infantile-onset disease with exudative retinal vasculopathy (Coats disease) and hearing loss, threatening irreversible visual loss.
Symptoms of nocturnal hypoventilation or respiratory insufficiency in advanced, wheelchair-dependent patients.
New or worsening foot drop causing recurrent falls.
Rapidly progressive or strikingly symmetrical weakness, which should prompt reconsideration of the diagnosis.
reference.prognosis: Progression is usually slow with wide variability; most patients remain ambulant and life expectancy is generally normal, although a minority become wheelchair dependent. Earlier onset and larger repeat contractions (fewer residual D4Z4 units) tend to predict more severe disease.
pitfalls: Marked asymmetry may be mistaken for a focal or acquired disorder rather than a genetic dystrophy.
A normal creatine kinase does not exclude the diagnosis.
Standard next-generation sequencing gene panels miss FSHD because the defect is a repeat contraction with an epigenetic mechanism; dedicated D4Z4 sizing and methylation testing are required.
Treatable extramuscular complications such as retinopathy and hearing loss are easily overlooked, particularly in children.
An absent family history is common because of de novo mutations and mosaicism and should not deter genetic testing.
references: Consensus diagnostic and care guidelines for facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy
management: No targeted therapy is currently available, so management centres on supportive and rehabilitative care
Individualised physiotherapy and moderate aerobic and resistance exercise to preserve function and limit contractures
Ankle-foot orthoses for tibialis anterior weakness and foot drop, with mobility aids to prevent falls
Scapulothoracic fixation surgery to improve arm elevation in selected disabling scapular winging
Symptomatic pain management and treatment of musculoskeletal complications

Monitoring for extramuscular disease with audiometry and dilated retinal examination, particularly in early-onset disease at risk of Coats retinopathy, plus respiratory assessment as weakness advances
Genetic counselling and cascade family testing, accounting for the digenic FSHD2 mechanism involving SMCHD1
